feat(self-update): verify the minisign-signed SHA256SUMS manifest before trusting any archive hash

`am self-update` compared the downloaded archive against an unsigned
SHA256SUMS fetched from the same release location as the archive, so
"Downloaded and verified" only meant "matches whatever manifest that
location served" — weaker than the installer's signed-manifest model
documented for v0.3.31+. Fixes #292.

- New `release_signing` module: a pure-Rust minisign verifier
  (ed25519-dalek + BLAKE2b-512 for the prehashed `ED` format, legacy
  `Ed` accepted) that checks both the file signature and the global
  signature over the trusted comment, exactly as `minisign -V` does. No
  minisign executable is required.
- The maintainer release key (id 1BBD79B28BF718D0, the key install.sh
  and install.ps1 pin) is embedded as a trusted-key list; a signature's
  key id selects the trusted key and an unknown id is refused, so key
  rotation is "trust both, sign with new, drop old". Debug builds honour
  AM_SELF_UPDATE_MINISIGN_PUBKEY for the mocked E2E suite; release
  builds refuse to run the updater when it is set.
- `download_and_verify_release` now downloads SHA256SUMS.minisig, fails
  closed on a missing/malformed/untrusted/tampered signature, and only
  then reads the archive digest from the authenticated manifest
  (exact-name match, sha256sum `*name` / `./name` forms accepted,
  digest must be 64 hex digits). Pre-v0.3.31 releases can no longer be
  installed by the updater; the error points at the installer.
- Tests: the published v0.3.32 SHA256SUMS + .minisig are checked in as
  a fixture and must verify with the embedded key; negative tests cover
  a one-byte manifest change, a substituted digest with the genuine
  signature, a tampered trusted comment, an untrusted key, a key-id
  collision, revocation, and malformed signature files.
  tests/e2e/test_self_update.sh signs its mock manifest with a generated
  minisign key and adds tampered-manifest and unsigned-manifest cases
  that assert the refusal and that the installed binaries are untouched.
- Docs: README, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG.
- legacy.rs: struct-init form for the fresh-process probe Config so
  `clippy --all-targets -D warnings` passes again (field_reassign_with_default),
  plus rustfmt.

fix(lint): drop the two clippy rules that never fired (#1262)

`clippy.toml` listed five reqwest constructors. Two of them --
`reqwest::Client::default` and `reqwest::ClientBuilder::default` -- do not
resolve, because `default` is a trait-impl item and `disallowed-methods`
matches inherent associated functions. Clippy said so on every build:

    warning: `reqwest::Client::default` does not refer to a reachable function
      --> clippy.toml:13:5
       = help: add `allow-invalid = true` to the entry to suppress this warning

So the config claimed to close four doors and closed three, and the comment
above the entries said the `Default` pair was covered "for the same reason"
as the rest. `tls_policy.rs` asserted parity between the two lanes by
comparing strings, which is exactly the check that cannot see the difference
between an entry clippy enforces and one it skips.

Verified against clippy 0.1.98 with a probe calling both constructors from a
non-allowlisted file: with all five entries present, `cargo clippy
--workspace --all-features -- -D warnings` exits 0 and reports nothing, while
the same probe using `Client::new()` fails as expected. The config warning is
emitted by the config loader rather than as a lint, so `-D warnings` never
escalated it and CI stayed green either way -- it was two warning lines per
build and no enforcement.

The doors themselves stay shut: `tls_policy.rs`'s scan covers all five
constructors, and reverting the fix in #1257 was caught by it. Its parity
test now checks both directions -- every lintable constructor is in
`clippy.toml`, and neither `Default` constructor is -- so re-adding an inert
entry fails the suite instead of printing a warning nobody reads.

Constraint: `disallowed-methods` resolves paths to functions; trait-impl items have no such path
Rejected: `allow-invalid = true` on both entries | silences the warning but leaves a rule that enforces nothing and reads as if it does
Rejected: qualified `<reqwest::Client as Default>::default` | verified on 0.1.98: accepted without resolving, so it warns about nothing and still never fires -- strictly worse, since it removes the only signal the entry is dead
Confidence: high
Scope-risk: narrow
Directive: the two `Default` constructors are enforced by `tls_policy.rs` alone; if a future clippy resolves trait-impl paths, add them back and delete the absence assertion in the same change
Not-tested: clippy versions other than 0.1.98

Done drawer orders by when an item was ticked, not its due date

The per-scope Done area sorted on the due date and never looked at doneTs,
so items verified on different days came back in no useful order. Every item
imported from a TODO.md carries no due date at all, so all of them tied - and
the comparator returned 1 for a tie instead of 0, which is inconsistent, so
V8 scrambled the whole all-tied run rather than leaving it alone.

Done now reads newest-ticked first: doneTs descending, then due date newest
first for items finished before completion stamps existed, and 0 for a real
tie so the list keeps its own order. Verified against the live 176-item list:
zero out-of-order pairs, day groups descending from today, unstamped items
last.

The tripwire that asserted "done rows sorted by due date" pinned the old
behaviour, so it is called out as a requirement change rather than quietly
loosened, and Feature 5 pins the new comparator with a negative needle
against the due-date-only one coming back.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Make the suite pass on every Python and configuration the package claims

CI had been failing on main before this branch and stayed failing after it,
with 23 reds across the version and platform matrix. Most were one of seven
causes, and several were real defects that only a machine unlike this one
could show.

requires-python is >=3.12, and three things only worked on 3.14. Seven bare
`Final` annotations raised "Plain typing.Final is not valid as type argument"
from get_type_hints on 3.12 and 3.13, so each now carries its type argument. A
functools.partial reached get_type_hints, which does not accept one before
3.14; partials are unwrapped to the callable they wrap, which also stops
callable_name answering "partial" and colliding two unnamed partials on one
MeTTa name. A test hardcoded 3.14's wording for `x // 0`, where 3.12 says
"integer division or modulo by zero"; it asks Python for the wording now.

Two generated or measured artifacts depended on the machine rather than the
source. fngen read a live engine, so a tree with libmork_ffi.so built emitted
mork-add-atoms and mork-flush and CI, which does not build it, read the
checked-in file as stale; the declarations are read from the Prolog that ships
either way, and their visibility from the list engine/spaces/catalog.pl owns.
scaling.py asked whether reader.so exists and then assumed mork-write routes
'foreign' regardless, reporting an unbuilt backend as a defect.

The profiler took the goal's answer with it when SWI's own report divided by a
zero tick count, which is what a short goal on a machine whose sampling timer
never fires collects. Only the report's failure is absorbed, and only once the
goal has answered; a zero_divisor from the profiled goal still raises.

ops.py held the frame inspect.currentframe() returned while calling onward,
making a cycle that kept an Answers view's engine cursor open until collection
ran. results.py, _space.py and _space_objects.py already released theirs.

test_workspace_paths reported git's own failure as a repository defect, and
looked only for a POSIX workspace root. Broadened to Windows drive paths, it
found two shipped comments carrying a personal home directory.

Verified: 2861 passed, 52 skipped, 1 xfailed; the Final and partial repairs
checked on python3.12.13 itself; fngen and the scaling gate run identically
with and without libmork_ffi.so; ruff passes.

Take each read model row's orgId from its own source record (#197) (#200)

The backfill script resolved one orgId with organization.findFirst() and
stamped it onto every row it wrote, while the queries fetched records across
all organisations with no filter. On a multi-org install that writes org B's
orders, shipments, carriers, customers and lanes into the read model tagged as
org A's, and the list endpoints filter on exactly that column. It is the failure
mode the security rule names, in a script rather than a route.

Invisible today because production has one organisation, and it stayed
invisible because the script was run by hand every few months. It now runs on
every deploy, so it is worth fixing before there is a second tenant rather than
after.

Each backfill now reads orgId off its own source row. The structural test that
already guarded this for issues covers the other five as well, plus an assertion
that organization.findFirst never comes back.

Also adds --only=<name> so a release can rebuild the read model it introduced
rather than all eight. An unknown name is refused with the list of valid ones,
because a backfill that silently does nothing looks exactly like one that
worked. Step selection lives in its own module: importing the script runs a
backfill as a side effect, which is not something a test should do.

Verified against a real database: the flag rebuilds 76 fulfilment orders on its
own, the full run still does all eight steps, and an unknown name fails loudly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014XpazBtdS6gbtrLPsibZjy

Also drops the trailing slash from the node_modules gitignore rule. With it, the
pattern matches directories only, so a node_modules symlink is not ignored and
walks into a commit. That nearly happened writing this one.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Make every boundary provable rather than inferred

The five things the marketplace review still wanted closed, in the order
they were raised:

Producer-side output caps. Every process now runs inside a wrapper that
caps its own stdout and stderr with head(1) before a byte reaches QML.
Truncating in an exit handler was always too late — by then this process
had already buffered whatever the command chose to write. The wrapper
exits with the wrapped command's own status, so timeout's 124 and every
real failure still arrive unchanged, and the probe caps each value it
collects individually, including the pre-existing all_proxy line it used
to import whole.

A bounded action queue. The queue holds state transitions, not a log of
clicks: a new transition replaces any pending one it makes obsolete, so
hammering the routing switch cannot leave a stale proxy or flags change
queued to replay later. At most one entry per kind can be waiting, with a
hard cap behind that.

The flags directory gate. Group-writable is a shared write, so mode 0770
no longer passes; the check reads owner and full mode, and the directory's
identity is pinned as device, inode, owner and mode and verified again
immediately before the replacement lands.

Proxy ownership. Whether this plugin may put a proxy setting back is now a
record it writes rather than a guess from the values matching. Before the
first mutation it stores the endpoint it is about to claim and, verbatim,
the settings it displaces; every mutation after that is checked and the
first failure rolls the whole transition back. Release touches only what
still matches the record, restores what was displaced, and then drops the
record — so a coincidentally matching proxy owned by another tool survives
untouched, and so does one that took over after we set ours.

Durability. The flags replacement and its directory entry are both fsynced
before a routing transition reports success.

feat(backfill): addressable over the API and from MCP

A backfill could only be created by an in-process CLI invocation, so a
server or an agent could not start, inspect, retry or cancel one.

The executor moved into the engine first, because that was the actual
blocker and the thing worth getting right: Louis's concern on #295 was a
backfill executor beside the normal durable-run path becoming a second
orchestration, and three surfaces each calling their own would have been
exactly that. The CLI is now a shell that prints and exits; the console
and MCP call the same function.

GET /api/backfills lists or fetches one; POST takes create, retry and
cancel. Create and retry are accepted and run on a thread, returning the
plan id immediately rather than holding a connection open for what can be
hours - the same shape as an asynchronous run, for the same reason.

A dry run writes nothing. "What would this queue" must not be a question
that queues anything, and there is a test asserting no plan is persisted.

Reading a backfill needs a viewer and changing one needs an operator,
named in the requirement table rather than left to the admin catch-all -
which would 403 every operator and log the action as "unknown".

The test pinning pool admission moved with the code it guards. Left in the
CLI it would have gone on passing about a file that no longer contains the
acquire.

integrate: 2.7.0 put the block in 25 skills and called it done

An audit of the whole surface -- every codelens command against every file that
could reference it -- says it was shallower than it looked.

The shared files knew nothing about it. Two resources are bundled into many
skills at once, and both had zero mentions, so the methodology said one thing
and the checklist another:

  review-skills-universal.md (495 lines, 6 skills) now opens with §0 EVIDENCE:
  which command settles which claim, the staleness rule, and the instruction to
  mark a degraded finding grep-depth. §1 layering, §4 N+1, §6 "untested" and §9
  dead code point back at it. A review is only worth the evidence under it, and
  most of that checklist is claims about reach.

  kb-steps.md (scan, rescan) gains golden rule 8: structural claims come from
  the graph where one exists, and the graph is an INPUT, never the output -- a
  fan-in number is not a business meaning, and the meaning is what a KB is for.
  _meta.yml records the resolution figure so a reader can tell a KB built on a
  resolved graph from one built on grep.

Two skills were excluded that should not have been. discover already asks
"which existing flow does this touch?" and qa-integration has to choose its own
regression set when no plan exists. Both are reach questions, and answering
either from intuition is the thing the block exists to stop. 27 of 30 now, and
the opt-out list records why the last three are genuinely out rather than merely
unvisited.

Staleness was missing from the contract. The shared paragraph said to confirm
with `codelens status` and never said to sync. An index built before the last
three commits answers confidently and wrongly, which is the worst failure this
integration has. All 27 blocks carry it now, with `codelens doctor` alongside:
low coverage from an uninstalled dependency and low coverage from a resolver
limit look identical in the number and are nothing alike in the fix.

node, callees and query were referenced nowhere and are now where they earn it
-- node in /namht-ask, callees in /namht-document, query in /namht-simplify.
Every codelens command is referenced by something except `mcp`, which is the
server's stdio entry point and is invoked by the client config, not a skill.

Both setup guides, the skills catalog, /namht-help and the VS Code README now
mention it. help is told NOT to run `codelens init` itself: that walks the whole
tree and is the user's decision.

README said 25 skills. It is 27.

en-US.ts overrides only the keys an American reader would otherwise read wrong,
so a value in it that agrees with en.ts agrees on purpose. It measures 0.00

Docker: CLI, custom image, volumes, user-defined network, Compose stack

All five parts run end to end with the output captured in docs/transcript.txt:
nginx pulled, run detached on 8080, inspected with exec, restarted, then
removed along with its image; a python:3.12-slim image built as
my-python-app:v1 and its layers read with docker history; MySQL data written,
the container destroyed, and the rows recovered by a new container on the same
named volume; two containers on a user-defined bridge reaching each other by
name; and a Flask backend behind an Nginx reverse proxy under Compose.

Two bugs came out of running it. The proxy reported unhealthy while serving
traffic perfectly: inside the nginx image localhost resolves to ::1 while
nginx bound 0.0.0.0:80 only, so the healthcheck was refused over IPv6
loopback. Fixed with listen [::]:80 and by pinning the check to 127.0.0.1,
since a healthcheck that depends on name resolution tests the resolver rather
than the service. It was not cosmetic: anything with depends_on
service_healthy on the proxy would never have started.

The second was mine. The first write-up asserted a 63.4MB pip layer and a
3.2kB COPY without reading docker history; the measured figures are 5.46MB and
4.1kB, and the transcript now carries the real numbers.

The transcript also proves the default bridge has no DNS (ping by container
name returns "bad address"), that the layer ordering makes a code edit reuse
the cached install, and that the proxy hop appears in the nginx and backend
logs from both ends. Every container is prefixed dbb- so teardown could never
touch the three unrelated containers running on this machine.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
The car arrives on its own clock, and the card names which state the feed is in (#140) (#154)

* The car arrives on its own clock, and the card names which state the feed is in (#140)

Phase 2 of #137. The VW portal now feeds the dashboard on a schedule, behind a
contract whose whole point is that the schedule is not the host's to choose.

IVehicleUpdateService has five members and no more: no credential abstraction,
no capability taxonomy, no auth-model enum. What it exposes about authentication
is not how a service authenticates but whether it currently can. NextDelay is
re-read after every fetch, because VW's portal is a fifteen-minute batch and
polling a sleeping Tesla costs its owner range -- no interval a host could pick
is right for both, so a backoff is the service moving its own number.

VwGroupUpdateService holds one session rather than replaying a password ninety-
six times a day, which reverses the reader's "sign in afresh every press" only
for the clock. Holding one is also the first thing that can measure one: #138
could not answer how long a portal session lives because nothing had ever kept
one, so the client gained a SignedIn event, the service times the gaps and logs
them, and the figure arrives from the reference install rather than a guess. A
lower bound by construction -- a session is found dead only when next used.

A refused password, a consent screen, an OTP or a missing data request stops the
feed asking altogether rather than retrying more slowly: the schedule would only
decide how fast the account gets locked, and the state that deserves attention
is the one an hourly retry would keep looking like weather. The /vehicle-portal
button, with its own fresh session, is the retry. NoDataAvailable is on the
other side of that line and does not even back off -- a new data request takes
hours to fill and backing off would take hours more to notice that it had.

Precedence lives in the composition root: with Vehicle:DataAct:Enabled on, the
MQTT worker is not registered at all, because "the manufacturer wins" cannot be
expressed against a last-write-wins holder any other way. Neither worker learns
about the other, and VehicleUpdateWorker logs the fact at startup -- an MQTT
feed publishing to a topic nobody subscribes to is otherwise silent.

The dashboard shows the car because it is defined, then which of four states its
feed is in. Stale and sign-in required are rendered differently on purpose: they
need opposite things from the owner, and a charger sitting idle is already the
most convincing impersonation of a fault this controller can produce. Home
Assistant gets Car feed -- Ok, Degraded or NeedsOwner, with the sentence as a
reason attribute -- published only where a feed exists.

Off by default, and having credentials is not switching it on. VehicleMqttWorker,
VehicleStateHolder, IVehicleTelemetry, VehicleState and MaxAge are untouched, and
a car with no update service configured behaves exactly as before, with tests
that say so.

Not yet run against the live portal on a clock: the session-lifetime line is what
the reference install will answer, which is why the instrumentation shipped with
the feature rather than after it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* A code from your mailbox is recognised for what it is, and a stopped feed keeps saying so (#140)

Two follow-ups on the same question: what happens when the portal asks for a
one-time code, and how anybody finds out.

The OTP guard had a hole. CanSignIn exists because this client is named "GIS
Consent Portal", so its ordinary email form says "consent" six times and the
prose needles alone aborted every sign-in -- but every rendered input counts
towards that guard, hidden ones included. An OTP page re-rendering the address
in a hidden email field would therefore have read as an ordinary sign-in page:
the identifier posted into a form wanting six digits, failing five pages later
as a refused password. Stopped correctly, for the wrong stated reason, which
sends the owner to their password instead of to their mailbox.

OneTimeCodeField closes it structurally, and is checked before the prose: a field
named otp or emailOtp says "a person is required" in every language a needle list
would otherwise have to be translated into. "code" is deliberately not in the
list -- it is OAuth's own parameter name, and a false positive would abort a
working sign-in, which is worse than the false negative it prevents.

And a state that never clears itself has to be said until it is fixed. Sign-in
required now shows as a band in the web UI's layout on every page rather than
only on the dashboard card it belongs to, as a Car feed row on Health where "is
anything wrong?" is actually asked, and as a warning in the log repeated every
six hours. The repetition is the point: a warning written once has scrolled out
of docker logs --tail by the time anybody reads it, and a stopped feed is
otherwise silent in a way indistinguishable from a parked car. It is a log line
and never a request, so "it stopped asking" stays literally true -- the test
asserts one fetch against three warnings.

The band sits inside AuthorizeView on the default policy, which is the audience
of every page except the sign-in one: that page goes on saying only the product
and the installation's name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* A capture time with nothing behind it is not a reading (#140)

Observed live on the reference install: the portal answered, the bundle parsed,
the capture time was minutes old -- and every value was blank, because not one
field name matched the vocabulary. The page reported that as a success and
showed a column of dashes.

Two things are wrong with calling it one. On the page it looks like a working
feed reporting a car that knows nothing about itself, which sends the reader
looking at the car instead of at the field names. And the update service would
write it to the holder: an empty VehicleState replacing a good reading, with an
age that resets to seconds old. The dashboard would show a car that had just
reported and had nothing to say.

"Absent is fine" (#73) was about a source that does not report a field. It was
never about a bundle in which every field is absent at once -- that is not a car
saying nothing, it is a vocabulary matching nothing. So a mapping that produces
no SOC, no range, no charge state, no plug state and no remaining time is now
UnusableData, and the message says how many fields the bundle carried.

The unrecognised names travel with the rejection, and the page lists them for a
failure as well as for a success. They used to hang off the success branch,
which put them exactly where they were least needed: this failure is the one
whose field list is the entire answer, and reporting "unusable data" while
holding the names back is a page keeping the diagnosis to itself.

UnusableData also stops being routed to NeedsOwner. It was arriving there via
IsWorthRetrying, which asks a different question -- a bundle nothing can read
wants a code change, not a browser, and the next delivery may well carry the
fields. It degrades, keeps asking, and the last good reading stands and ages.
The NeedsOwner set is now named outright rather than derived.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The page says what it recognised, not only what it did not (#140)

The first live bundle came back with 47 fields, 41 of them unrecognised -- and
the page could not say what the other six were or what they held. That is the
half of the diagnostic that was missing, and it is the half that decides what to
do next: a name absent from the unrecognised list means either "the bundle never
carried it" or "it carried it and the value was a sentinel that filtering threw
away", and those want opposite fixes. One is a name to add to VwGroupFieldNames;
the other is a car reporting the field empty, where no name would help.

So the mapper now reports the fields it matched with the newest raw value read
out of each -- sentinels included, quoted and untouched, because "" and "invalid"
are exactly what this exists to reveal -- and the page lists them beside the
names it did not match.

The second blind spot is worse because nothing hints at it. A report carrying no
timestamp this parser recognises is dropped whole, and every field in it is
dropped too -- including out of the unrecognised-names list, which is the one
place anybody would look. A battery report under a timestamp spelled a new way
is therefore indistinguishable from a bundle that never carried a battery. The
bundle reader now reports what it discarded and the field names that went with
it, on an overload so no existing caller changes.

Both surfaces on the same terms as the unmapped list itself: on the page,
whether the read succeeded or failed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The battery's energy content is visible, and a failed read describes its delivery (#140)

The reference ID.4's live delivery settles what the first one only hinted at.
Two fields matched and both held real values -- settings.target_soc "80" and
mileage.value "53065" -- so the vocabulary is not broken and nothing was a
sentinel. What that bundle carries is a vehicle-status report: locks, windows,
parking lights, climate consumption, charge-mode settings, error codes. There is
no state of charge in it at all, and no range, plug state or charging state.

The only battery figures in it are energy_contents.current_energy_content and
its maximal sibling, and those are now recognised so their values show. Not read:
dividing one by the other would produce a state of charge we computed rather than
one the car reported, and that is a decision about what SocPercent means. It
wants the numbers in front of somebody first, which is what listing them does.

A failed read now also describes the delivery it failed on -- the car, the
snapshot count and the span. On a mapping failure that is half the diagnosis: it
is what tells "this quarter-hour said nothing" apart from "the portal is handing
us one report type per delivery and the battery is in another one". The block
was in the success branch, which is where it was least useful.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* One reading, assembled from as many deliveries as it takes (#140)

The first live read settled what the fixtures could not. The reference ID.4's
newest delivery carried 47 fields -- a real odometer (53,065), a real charge
target (80), doors, windows, parking lights, climate consumption, charge-mode
settings, error codes -- and no state of charge, no range, no plug state and no
charging state. Nothing was a sentinel and nothing was misspelled: the vocabulary
matched what was there. The battery was not in that delivery.

That is what type=partial means, and it had been read as "the newest delivery is
the car". It is not: each delivery carries the reports that changed, so which
report type arrives is a coin toss.

So a read now merges deliveries, adaptively. Newest first; older ones only while
the merged reading still has no state of charge; never more than
Vehicle:DataAct:MaxDatasetsPerRead, four by default, which is an hour of a
fifteen-minute request and the span over which a parked car's SOC does not
meaningfully move. A car whose newest delivery carries the battery downloads
exactly one ZIP, as before -- the budget is a ceiling, not a cost. Merging needed
no new rules: several snapshots, sentinels filtered first, newest real value wins
is what the mapper was already built to do, which is why #139 wrote those
tie-breaks before anything needed them.

What merging does make load-bearing is the dating. A reading used to be stamped
with the newest snapshot in the pile; within one delivery that is minutes of
slack, but across merged deliveries it is the difference between honest and not.
A state of charge from 10:14 wearing a 10:29 status report's clock is a stale
reading with a fresh face, and freshness is the one thing this feed exists to let
an owner judge. A reading is now dated by the newest snapshot that contributed a
value to it.

The button and the feed share one path for all of this: VwGroupPortalClient.
ReadAsync, which the reader had been duplicating step by step. The reader keeps
what it alone needs -- the reporting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The reading is dated by its state of charge, and the energy contents are not one (#140)

The first successful live read answered both of the questions it raised.

The energy contents are NOT a state of charge. They were surfaced precisely to
find out whether a percentage could be divided out of them for a delivery that
carries no SOC of its own. The car answered: 328.5 of 738.0 is 44.5%, against the
50 that the same read's battery_state_report.soc reported. The units are not
kilowatt-hours and the pair does not describe the same quantity the percentage
does -- a reserve below the usable window would explain it. Shipping that division
on the plausibility of the names would have been wrong by five and a half points,
silently, in the number every kilowatt-hour target is computed from. They stay
recognised and unread, which is what KnownButUnused is for.

And the merge budget's justification was wrong in a way that mattered. "Four
deliveries is an hour of a fifteen-minute request" -- the portal then offered
thirty deliveries whose newest four spanned most of a day, because it delivers
when the car reports rather than on a clock. So a state of charge can be hours
older than the status report merged beside it, and dating the pair by the newer
of them shows an old percentage as minutes fresh.

The reading is now dated by the state of charge's own snapshot, falling back to
the newest contributing field only when there is no SOC at all. Everything else
on a VehicleState is display; the percentage is what a target is computed from
and what MaxAge is judged against, so it is the field the timestamp belongs to.
The budget bounds what a read costs over a domestic uplink and says nothing about
how old the answer is -- the answer says that itself.

The delivery span on the page shows dates when its two ends disagree about the
day, because "16:30 - 10:29" reads as a fault rather than as most of a day.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* Field names and their values stop overlapping (#140)

Reported from the live page: in the recognised-fields list the two columns ran
into each other. Reproduced in a browser against the real stylesheet -- the name
"energy_contents.maximal_energy_content.physical_value" sits straight on top of
its value.

The list was using .facts, whose first column is minmax(8rem, max-content). That
is right for "Battery" and "Odometer" and wrong here, where the LABEL is the
data: a fifty-character dotted path sizes the column past the panel. Grid items
also default to min-width:auto, so an unbreakable token cannot shrink -- which is
why it overlapped rather than wrapped.

So this list gets its own shape. .fields is a proportional two-column grid whose
cells may shrink (min-width: 0) and wrap (overflow-wrap: anywhere), stacking into
one column on a phone, where two columns of dotted paths are unreadable however
they wrap.

Wrapping "anywhere" then broke mid-word -- current_charge_st / ate -- so each dot
and underscore now carries a <wbr>, and the wrap lands on a joint. That means the
page emits markup where it emitted text, so every segment is HTML-encoded on the
way through and a test pins it: a field name is a string from the portal, and
this is the only place one reaches the browser as markup.

Verified by screenshotting the real stylesheet at 1100px and 420px rather than by
reasoning about the CSS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The Health page says whether the feed is running, not only whether it works (#140)

Validating the service meant grepping a container log for two things: is it
reading on its own clock, and is it holding one session? Both are now on the page
that exists to answer "is anything wrong?".

Three rows beside Car feed. Feed reads -- readings of attempts, and how long ago
the last one landed -- which separates "the feed is fine" from "the feed has been
failing quietly for an hour". Portal session: its age and the number of sign-ins
since start, where ONE is the healthy answer however long the controller has been
up, and more is the session-expiry measurement #138 could not make, said in
words. Next read, which reads "never -- the feed has stopped" when blocked, so a
stopped feed cannot look like a slow one.

Through IVehicleFeedDiagnostics, a second interface rather than five more members
on IVehicleUpdateService. That contract stays as small as #140 left it: what
every feed must answer is whether it can produce a reading. A session age and a
next-due time are facts about a polling feed with a held session -- a push-based
one has neither -- so they are offered by the services that have them and asked
for with a type test by the one page that cares. A feed offering none is not
described with a row of zeroes, which would read as one that had never run.

* Where a snapshot spells the state of charge twice, the listed preference decides (#140)

Found while chasing a portal reading that disagreed with the car. Not the cause
of that -- the reference bundle carries one spelling -- but a real bug behind it.

The candidate lists are ordered on purpose. battery_level_HV.value leads because
a real bundle carries it with its own .state beside it, and hv_soc trails because
it is documented and this car does not send it. That order decided nothing:
within one snapshot the picker walked the values dictionary and returned the
first field matching ANY candidate, so the winner was whichever name the portal
happened to serialise first.

It costs nothing on a bundle carrying one spelling, which is every bundle seen so
far, and would have been an unreproducible wrong number on the first one that
carried two -- with the two agreeing most of the time, which is worse.

Newest snapshot still wins over candidate order: a newer reading of the same
quantity beats a preferred name for an older one. The preference now decides
within a snapshot, which is where it was always meant to.

Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The newest reading wins, whichever feed produced it (#140)

Not the answer to "the portal says 60 and the car says 69" -- that is a channel
question and is being chased separately -- but the enabling piece, and a fix in
its own right.

VehicleStateHolder now keeps the reading with the newest capture time and ignores
an older one. Two sources can therefore feed one car without a race, which was
previously prevented by not registering the MQTT worker at all whenever the
manufacturer service was on. That exclusion was the issue's "if both sources are
on, the manufacturer service wins", and the reference install showed why deciding
it in advance is the wrong shape: the Data Act portal's state of charge for that
car is coarser and later than the same manufacturer's live channel. Which source
is better is a fact about a car and a moment, not something a registration can be
right about once. A feed that stops stops advancing, so the other takes over
within one reading and precedence corrects itself.

It also fixes something that was always there: a retained MQTT message replayed
on reconnect no longer overwrites a fresher reading with a stale one.

And the diagnostics gain the field that would have shortened this hunt: every
recognised field now carries the moment the CAR reported it, not just its value.
A read merges several deliveries, so two figures on that page can be hours apart
-- comparing them without their times is how a coarse reading and a stale one get
mistaken for each other, which is exactly what happened.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* A car is the whole set of reports, not the first one with a battery in it (#140)

Reported from the live page: the battery came back correct and Range, Charging,
Plug and Time left all went blank at once.

The merge stopped as soon as a state of charge turned up. That reasoning came
from "the reading the feed exists for", and it is wrong about this portal for the
same reason the merge exists at all: the partial deliveries are split BY REPORT
TYPE. The battery is in one, the charging state and the remaining time in
another, the plug in a third. Stopping at the first percentage therefore produced
a card with a battery and four dashes -- worse than before merging existed, since
before it those older deliveries were being read anyway.

So a read now merges while the reading is still short of anything a VehicleState
can hold, and stops early only when it has the lot. MaxDatasetsPerRead is what
stops it on a car that never reports a plug state, and the log says what a read is
still short of when the budget runs out -- the only way to know whether raising it
would buy anything rather than four more downloads.

The cost is honest and now documented as such: a delivery carrying a whole car is
still one download, and a car whose reports are split will spend most of the
budget every read.

Signed-off-by: Martin Pospisil <m.pospisil76@gmail.com>

* The page names the report types it merged, and what is still absent (#140)

Battery, charging state and remaining time now arrive; range and plug state do
not. That is two different problems wearing one face -- no report I have carries
them, or the report that would is one this read did not reach -- and they want
opposite responses: a wider budget, against accepting that this car does not send
them at all.

So a read names the report types it merged, from the bundles' own report_type
field, and says what the reading is still short of and how many of the available
deliveries it took to get there. Raising MaxDatasetsPerRead and pressing the
button once is then a measurement rather than a guess: if a much wider read still
finds no range, the answer is that the Data Act channel does not carry one for
this car -- which is what the ID.4 capture committed in #139 already suggested,
having no range field either.

No vocabulary was added on suspicion. Nothing in the fifty unrecognised names
from the reference car looks like a range or a plug, and adding hopeful spellings
would only make the next absence harder to read.

* The merge budget can actually be set (#140)

Both the page and the log tell an owner to raise MaxDatasetsPerRead when a
reading is still short of a field. Nothing bound it. It was a constant on the
options object that no configuration could reach, so following that advice
changed nothing -- the worst kind of wrong, because it looks like the answer
failing rather than the instruction being broken. Found by writing the
instruction out for somebody about to follow it.

Vehicle:DataAct:MaxDatasetsPerRead now binds, with VW_MAX_DATASETS beside it on
the same terms as the other four, through the compose file and both .env
examples.

A value that is not a positive count is refused at startup naming the key, rather
than clamped back to the default: a typo that silently becomes 4 is the same
afternoon of wondering by another route.

* A 429 is the portal asking for less, not a bundle that cannot be read (#140)

Pressing the button a few times in a row, twelve deliveries deep, was answered
with 429 Too Many Requests on the delivery endpoint. Three things were wrong with
what happened next.

It was classified as UnusableData, so the page said "pressing again will not
help. This one needs something changed, or a browser." Every part of that is
false for a rate limit: nothing is broken, no browser is involved, and the fix is
to wait. 429 is now Transient -- retryable by contract -- and where the portal
sends Retry-After the message quotes it, so the wait is known rather than
guessed. For the feed that is the difference between Degraded with a backoff and
a NeedsOwner that stops asking for good.

Worse, one refused download discarded the whole read. A deep merge that had
already assembled a battery, a charging state and a remaining time threw all of
it away because the EXTRA delivery it was trying to improve on was refused. A
delivery that never arrives can only have added to what is in hand, so the merge
now ends there and reports what it has, with a note saying why it stopped short.

And the burst was ours. The deliveries are the only place this client makes
several requests at one endpoint in a row, so they are now spaced a second apart
-- three seconds on a four-deep read every fifteen minutes, nothing at all on the
common single-delivery case, and the difference between asking for a lot and
asking rudely.

fix(broker): stop an orphaned receipt from jamming a parked agent forever (#1639)

* fix(broker): stop an orphaned receipt from jamming a parked agent forever

A `manual_flush` queue stamps each held message with the `agent_id` that
was live when it was queued, and the flush gate looked that cursor up by
`receipt.agent_id`. That key is not stable: `bind_authoritative_identity`
(spawn register, token identity resolve, inventory repair) retires the
previous `agent_id` and drops its cursor, and a node-control resume
handshake's `seed_cursor` moves the cumulative position to Relaycast's
own. Either event left already-parked receipts pointing at a cursor that
could never accept them.

`can_ack_receipt` returned false for that case, which is indistinguishable
from "not ACKable yet", so the flush stopped at the head message forever.
`flushed: 0`, and a partial flush deliberately pins the worker back into
`manual_flush`, so every later DM parked behind the poisoned head. The
agent went permanently deaf while `send_dm` kept returning
`recipientMatched: true` (relay#1593, relay#1559).

Split the gate into `receipt_ackability` -> Ready / Blocked / Orphaned.
Orphaned messages are injected and dropped without an ACK: Relaycast keeps
ownership of the frame so its redelivery policy is untouched. Withholding
the ACK was always the safe half; withholding the message was the bug. A
genuine ordering gap still classifies Blocked and still holds the queue.

Tradeoff: an orphaned frame Relaycast later redelivers under the new
identity can now be seen twice. Duplicate delivery beats permanent
deafness, and the old behaviour bought nothing here since a retired
identity is never redelivered to.

Also surface the failure. `POST /api/spawned/{name}/flush` returned a bare
count while `flush_result.failure` went only to a `tracing::warn!`, so
`node agent message flush` printed `{"flushed": 0}` with no error. That
ambiguity is why the flush evidence on relay#1593 was retracted as "0 is
the expected answer and proved nothing" -- it was a swallowed failure, not
a null result. The route now returns `held` and `blocked_reason` too.

Verified red then green with a byte-identical probe:
  red  (source at origin/main): 2 FAILED, left: 0 / right: 2
  green (fix applied):          8 passed; 0 failed
The guards `manual_flush_still_stops_on_a_genuine_sequence_gap` and
`manual_flush_failure_retains_failed_message_and_suffix_without_ack` pass
in both directions, so ordering is still enforced.

The trigger is a duplicate spawn that is itself REJECTED. `workers.spawn` bails

spawn survives only because agent names collide"). Those duplicate dispatches

subscriptions.name: rottenSSHrimp
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Cles SSH FIDO2 dans le Credential Manager, version 1.3

Un identifiant « FIDO2 security key » enrole une cle SSH sur un token
(YubiKey ou autre): le document ne garde qu'un key handle, le secret ne
quitte jamais le token, et chaque connexion exige un toucher. Types
OpenSSH sk-ssh-ed25519 et sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, choisis selon ce que
le token annonce; serveur OpenSSH >= 8.2. Copy SSH ID et Rotate
marchent comme pour une cle geree logicielle.

Aucun patch de libssh2: libssh2_userauth_publickey_sk (1.11, backend
OpenSSL) lit la cle privee sk, nous rappelle pour la signature et
fabrique lui-meme le blob « sig || flags || counter ». Le symbole est
resolu en option, le binding libfido2 ne leve jamais: sans la lib,
l'application demarre et seuls ces identifiants sont indisponibles.
sig_r/sig_s sont alloues avec le malloc C, libssh2 les libere avec le
free de son runtime.

Windows passe par le peripherique virtuel windows://hello (API WebAuthn,
pas de droits administrateur): c'est Windows qui demande le geste et le
PIN, et il n'y a pas de sondage muet possible -- OpenSSH fait pareil.
Windows Hello n'annonce aucun algorithme, d'ou ECDSA de ce cote et
Ed25519 ailleurs; le type est fige dans la cle et voyage avec le
document, un .rsh sert donc sur les trois OS avec le meme token. Apres
enrolement, l'AAGUID dit si la cle a ete creee dans le TPM du poste au
lieu du token amovible: l'utilisateur est prevenu, elle ne suivrait pas
le document.

Schema v11 (auth_type 'fido_key'). Le sceau du document connait la
nouvelle version dans les DEUX case: uRshSchema et
uRshDocument.CanonicalQueriesFor, sans quoi le commit de la migration
levait « unknown schema version » et tout document anterieur passait
pour endommage. Verifie avec un document v10 contenant une cle geree:
tout ressort intact.

Packaging: fido2.dll + cbor.dll (vcpkg, meme baseline que FreeRDP, lies
a libcrypto-3-x64.dll et z.dll deja livrees -- un seul OpenSSL, la ou
l'archive Yubico en apportait un second); libfido2 dans le bundle macOS,
Recommends pour le .deb, optdepends pour Arch. Licences BSD-2 et MIT
jointes.

subscriptions.last_commit_message: 7.23.46: the bytes a node owns but cannot hold, and a missing one said out loud A treedb node often owns something that is not JSON -- a photo, a plan, a clip -- and the SDK's C_ASSETS (7.17.0) keeps those bytes in a directory it owns while the node names one with an fkey. `get-asset` answers either with a signed url or with the bytes inline, and the BACKEND decides which: a node with a web server in front of its store gets the fast, cacheable form, one without still shows its images instead of showing nothing. `yui_asset.js` is the two ends of that, and it deliberately does NOT talk to the backend: asking is an action and belongs in the view's own FSM. yui_asset_id/ids read a single-valued fkey, an array fkey and an expanded ref; yui_asset_src turns either answer into one src; yui_asset_element builds the element from the CONTENT TYPE THE BACKEND STORED -- img, video or audio, because video and audio are assets too and an whose src is a film shows the very broken box this removes. It used to leave a broken box and no word about it, indistinguishable from a slow one and from a bug -- 47 such holes in one day on artgins.ytreedb.com before anybody noticed. yui_asset_element wires onerror so the dead element is REPLACED by a marker, whatever the reason: an expired signature, a blob gone from the store, an unsupported codec. yui_asset_src answers null and never "" for an unusable answer: reloads the page in some browsers, which is a worse failure than the one being reported. subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(github): stop gh-release-delete matching delete-asset, --help, and quoted search text

Fixes #380.

`platform.github:gh-release-delete` ended in `delete\b`, and `\b` sits
between `delete` and `-`, so the rule also fired on the sibling command
`gh release delete-asset` — including `gh release delete-asset --help` —
and explained it as deleting the whole release. Two more shapes of the
same report: `--help` on any guarded `gh` command was denied even though
gh prints usage and exits before any API call, and quoted search text
(`gh search issues 'gh release delete'`) matched the unanchored regex.

- Every verb in the pack now ends in `(?![\w-])` instead of `\b`, so a
  hyphenated sibling subcommand can never inherit a rule.
- `gh release delete-asset` is its own rule, `gh-release-delete-asset`
  (Medium), with an asset-specific explanation and suggestions.
- Help is a pack safe pattern: `--help` anywhere before a bare `--`,
  `-h` (except under `repo edit`, where `-h` is `--homepage`), and
  `gh help <cmd>`. Quoted tokens are consumed whole and the walk stops at
  redirection characters, so `'v1 --help'`, `-- --help`, and
  `--yes > --help` still fall through to the destructive rules.
- The argument sanitizer treats `gh search <kind> ...` as query data and
  registers `gh -S/--search`; the Cmd-dialect overlay mirrors the
  `gh search` rule so all four dialects agree.

Regression coverage: pack unit tests, sanitizer unit tests, a
cross-pack FP corpus file (#380) with true-positive controls, and the
backtracking audit map; docs/packs/platform.md regenerated.
